newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: International agencies in $133 mln Afghan appeal.
newsitem.headline: International agencies in $133 mln Afghan appeal.

text.p: International aid organisations launched an appeal on Tuesday to raise $133 million for emergency humanitarian relief in war ravaged Afghanistan.
"The $133 million that we are requesting is a drop in the ocean of the needs of the country," Alfredo Witschi-Cestari, U.N. co-ordinator for humanitarian assistance in Afghanistan, said on Tuesday.
"It is nothing compared to the real needs, but it can make the difference between a life-threatening situation and a life-sustaining situation," he said.
After 17 years of war, Afghanistan is among the world's most needy countries.
"By any international comparison, the scale of need in Afghanistan is daunting," the appeal document said.
"More land mines are buried in Afghanistan than in any other country in the world. As many as 10 Afghan fall victims to mines daily," it said.
Afghanistan also has the highest rate of infant, childhood and maternal mortality in Asia.

The document said the funds raised would be used for "nation-wide programmes that respond to the immediate needs across Afghanistan, including basic relief activities, mine clearance, assistance to the disabled, repatriation, immunisation and narcotics control.
Past appeals for assistance in Afghanistan have met with a disappointing response. An appeal for $124 million in 1995/96 raised $56 million.
Witschi-Cestari said that if the appeal does not reach the target for 1997, aid officials will face difficult decisions.
"If we have a low response to the 1997 appeal, we will have to make choices that will represent further hardship for the people who are in need of assistance." he said.
He conceded that there was a danger that policies of the purist Islamic Taleban, particularly those concerning women, might make donors less willing to give money.
The Taleban took control of the capital Kabul in late September, giving the Islamic group control of more than two thirds of the country.
The group are now battling against the forces of the ousted government and a powerful northern leader.
Under Taleban rule, girl's schools have been closed and women banned from the workplace.

"In 1997, we are particularly worried because of the issue concerning the treatment of women by the Taleban. Many donors have expressed their worry and mentioned the possibility that they will cut their financial support if women are not benefiting, or if women are not involved." he said.
But Witschi-Cestari said he believed that the United Nations had a duty to remain in Afghanistan.
"I believe that we should not accept conditions that are against the basic principles of human rights, but we should not simply turn our backs," he said.

The appeal document said that the aid community would be negotiating to overcome any "differences of approach" with the authorities. But warned if dialogue failed certain programmes could be put in jeopardy.
A number of aid organisations have already suspended some of their programmes because of the policies of the Taleban concerning women.
